10399-the-story-of-louis-riel-the-rebel-:
Joseph Edmond Collins published this biography in Toronto in 1885, soon after Louis Riel's rebellion and trial. Collins calls Riel an apostle of insurrection, yet insists on doing him justice, even while condemning the misery and blood his career caused. The book follows Riel along the Red River, a land long marked by war.

Collins traces Riel's father, also Louis, born at La Crosse in the North-West, and his son's rise among Metis and settlers. Plains, Chippewa and Sioux wars, and the name Red River frame the story. Readers get a vivid, period Canadian account of a rebel chief, partisan in tone but rich in detail.
14091-barkham-burroughs-encyclopaedia-of:
Barkham Burroughs published this treasure-house in 1889 for young and old alike, promising answers to every everyday question. Inside sit 521 recipes, 236 remedies, 150 themes for debate, advice on handsome looks, Mother Shipton's prophecy, a cure for baldness, and how to tell death. Twenty thousand things worth knowing round out the boast, with pictures of the world's tallest buildings.

History and household lore mix freely. A long passage follows plague from the Orient to Constantinople, Sicily, Avignon, and Dorset in 1348, with earthquakes, floods, and locust clouds as possible companions. Kitchen pages then teach jarred herrings, broiled herrings, and fried herrings in careful steps. Readers dipped in anywhere, and the book charms today as a Victorian browser's delight: useful, credulous, and gloriously miscellaneous.
1499-beacon-lights-of-history-volume-3-p:
John Lord's second part of his third volume turns from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance and Reformation. Through great figures of art, learning, and faith, Lord traces how Europe woke from medieval sleep to new learning, new churches. New nations, with beacon lights marking each stage of the road.

The manner is the same as in Part 1: clear lectures, moral judgments, and vivid anecdotes for general readers. The volume pairs with the Middle Ages part to complete a survey of a thousand years. It is an old-fashioned but engaging guide to an age of upheaval.
16335-essays-on-the-stage-preface-to-the:
This slim 1948 reprint pairs two rare prefaces from the late 1600s, both on the stage and its defense. Thomas D'Urfey's preface to The Campaigners (1698) comes first, followed by an anonymous preface to a translation of Bossuet's Maxims and Reflections upon Plays (1699). Joseph Wood Krutch supplies the introduction.

Issued by the Augustan Reprint Society, the booklet serves scholars of Restoration drama and early stage debate. The two texts argue from opposite sides about what plays may do and why they matter. Short as it is, the volume gives a direct taste of a fierce old quarrel over the theater.
21694-the-prairie-chief:
Whitewing, a thinker among his tribe, leads R. M. Ballantyne's The Prairie Chief on the North American plains. He is no chief of the highest standing, yet his people hold him a great man. Courage, strength, and speed are the least of his gifts in their eyes.

Whitewing ponders the Great Manitou and the affairs of life with a deep mind. He disbelieves in revenge, a duty and pleasure to most of his fellows. He will not deck himself with trophies of his prowess, though he faces the grizzly bear. Ballantyne gives his hero a modesty that puzzles young braves and wins their veneration.
23217-the-roll-call-of-the-reef: The Roll Call of the Reef turns on a curious object. Its narrator studies the body of a lock made of half a dozen brass rings, set edge to edge with great care. Rubbing the brass with a thumb, he finds that each of the six rings carries a series of letters engraved around it.
2329-autobiography-of-a-pocket-handkerch:
James Fenimore Cooper tries a playful experiment: the life story of a pocket handkerchief, from flax field to ballroom to battlefield. Autobiography of a Pocket-Handkerchief follows its heroine's owner through French society, with the handkerchief observing manners, morals, and vanity along the way. The conceit lets Cooper satirize fashion and class.

The tale is slight but witty, and its object narrator anticipates later experiments in fiction. Readers will smile at its ingenuity even where the satire feels dated. It is a curiosity for Cooper completists and lovers of odd narrators.
26109-hail-to-the-chief:
Sam and Janet Argo's political novel opens in a convention hall roaring for Cannon, whose buttons read 'Blast 'em With Cannon!' and 'Cannon Can Do!' Delegates, spectators, and first-time voters merge into one surging crowd as favorite sons fall away and the party's new candidate takes the floor.

Headlines trace Cannon's later wars with the CIA order, the Budget Bureau, and the Treasury, then a stroke and a resignation. Abroad, Uganda splits, Ruanda-Urundi neighbors eye territory, and a Soviet voice at the United Nations blames imperialist agents, while vice-presidential candidate Matthew Fisher calls both Ugandas communist-controlled. The tale mixes campaign noise with Cold War crisis.
27012-the-farmer-boy-and-how-he-became-c:
The Farmer Boy, and How He Became Commander-in-Chief, by Uncle Juvinell and edited by William M. Thayer, tells young readers how George Washington grew from a farm boy into a commander. Published in Boston in 1864, it reached its seventh thousand in print.

Thayer's introduction recalls his earlier promise of a farmer boy volume, now fulfilled by another pen. The story follows Washington's boyhood work, his journeys by river and horseback toward the Forks of the Ohio, and the early training that shaped the man who would lead an army.
283-the-reef:
George Darrow crosses to Dover reading Anna Leath's telegram: unexpected obstacle, do not come till the thirtieth. Edith Wharton's Reef follows Darrow as Anna twice puts him off, then welcomes him into a tangle of old lovers and new claims. Her daughter Effie and the young Sophy Viner complicate matters.

Wharton tracks motive and manners with cool precision, letting a delayed arrival expose a marriage bargain. Darrow, Anna, and Sophy each hide a past that the others guess. The novel's title reef is the moral hazard beneath polite talk. It ranks among Wharton's subtlest studies of love.
28566-hollyhock-a-spirit-of-mischief:
L. T. Meade's Hollyhock, a Spirit of Mischief, published by W. and R. Chambers of London and Edinburgh in 1916, contrasts two glens. The Lower Glen is poor, its people hard-working and humble, while the Upper Glen, fifty miles from Edinburgh and Glasgow, is broad, flat, and sheltered by mountains. Two families live there: Mrs. Constable at the Paddock and her brother at the Garden.

The Hon. George Lennox calls his five daughters by flower names, including Hollyhock, whose baptismal name is Jacqueline. Mrs. Constable names her five boys for precious stones. Chapters follow Aunt Agnes, a great school, a great conspiracy, fire spirits, and Hollyhock's deed of valour. Readers get a girls' tale of mischief turned to courage.
35823-the-secret-of-the-reef:
Harold Bindloss wrote The Secret of the Reef, copyrighted in 1914. Bindloss had written Thurston of Orchard Valley and By Right of Purchase. A colour front plate shows Clay, who had lost control of his limbs.

Jimmy Farquhar, second mate, stands on a liner crossing the North Pacific by moonlight as the tale opens. Chapters move fast from his dismissal: a new venture, the fury of the sea, an island, and grubstakes. A mine at Snowy Creek and the wreck of the Kanawha follow. The strong-room, bogus gold, and a dangerous secret fill the middle. The hidden gold and a gift from the dead close the story.
36470-photographs-of-nebul-and-clusters-:
Photographs of Nebulae and Clusters Made with the Crossley Reflector forms Volume Eight of the Publications of the Lick Observatory, issued at Sacramento in 1908. A note from the observatory at Mount Hamilton in November 1908 heads the volume. Plate Ten shows the Great Nebula in Orion. The Regents of the University of California passed the work.

The note warns of faint dark rings round stars in two plates. Rings in subjects ten and twelve look stronger in print than in first proofs, it says. Steel facing and printing seem to have raised the effect. The engraver may have made it worse. To reprint would have held the book for weeks, so the flaw was left. The volume holds large plates of star clouds and clusters for star study.
36603-the-yellow-chief:
The Yellow Chief is a frontier novel by Captain Mayne Reid, in an edition published by George Routledge and Sons in 1875. The tale opens on a cotton plantation not far from Vicksburg, Mississippi, with an order for a punishment.

Blount Blackadder, the eighteen-year-old son of the plantation's owner, commands the overseer to take a young slave to the pump and give him a double dose. The victim is about Blount's own age and size, but his tawny skin and short crisped hair mark him as a mulatto, and a slave. The pump punishment, Reid explains, pours a continuous stream of cold water on the head until it feels as though the skull were splitting. Reid sets the scene twenty years before his telling, in the slave South his adventure tales often crossed.
36723-one-maid-s-mischief:
One Maid's Mischief is a novel by George Manville Fenn, published in London by Ward and Downey in an edition dated 1887. The first chapter is called One of Her Victims. It opens at seven on a May morning, with a thrush waking the echoes.

Blackbirds whistle in the copse, and a chaffinch pours notes from the pink blossomed apple trees. Larks rival each other above the young corn and clover. Heavy dew lies on the wallflowers, with a whisper of frost in the shade. The Reverend Arthur Rosebury stands contemplating the rectory flower beds. Fenn builds the scene before the mischief begins, in his ample Victorian manner. The maid of the title will stir this quiet parish world, and her victims are promised from the first page.
38104-english-secularism-a-confession-of:
George Jacob Holyoake set out his confession of belief in 1896, in pieces first run in The Open Court. His preface is dated at Brighton in February of that year. The new free thought called Secularism, he says, holds neither theism nor atheism within it. Contrast, he holds, is the bright light of argument.

The publisher's word calls him the brain of the party in England. He coined the name Secularism and stood at the back of its work from the start. He feared neither prison, nor black looks, nor any harm for the cause. The book tells what the creed holds and what it leaves open, for readers on both sides of the sea.
40767-old-plantation-days-being-recollec:
Old Plantation Days is a book of memories of southern life before the Civil War, by Mrs. N. B. De Saussure. It came out in New York in 1909 from Duffield and Company. A note by the author states its rise. The memories are published at the call of many friends, she says. They had read the work in draft and urged that the memories be given a more lasting form and a wider reach.

The book opens as a letter to the author's granddaughter Dorothy. Grandmother is growing to be an old lady, it begins. Dorothy is still too young to— as the first lines break off. A note states that mixed spellings and hyphens of the first print have been kept, and clear slips of print set right. The work is a first-hand record of the old South by one who lived in it.
45169-the-autobiography-of-a-thief:
Hutchins Hapgood set down The Autobiography of a Thief, issued at New York in 1903. Hapgood met the man, a past pickpocket and burglar, and wrote his life in his own voice. Two quotes, from Faust and from Bacon, head the book. Fourteen chapters trace the life.

Chapters move from boyhood and first crime to ward life in New York. Graft, theft of bonds, and the risks of burglary fill the middle. Long parts tell of prison, in and out, more than once. A mad house stay and a hard climb out close the tale. The book gives a plain first hand view of crime and jail in that time.
45402-the-insurgent-chief:
The Insurgent Chief is a novel by Gustave Aimard, published in London by J A Berger of Catherine Street. Aimard also wrote Queen of the Savannah and The Red Track. He specialized in adventure tales of the Americas, drawn from his own wandering years.

The story is set in and around San Miguel de Tucuman, in Argentina. Book one is called The Pincheyras and book two The Montonero. The opening describes the Callejon de las Cruces, a narrow street ending at the river. One great house there, barred like a prison, serves as a retreat for pious women. Around that house of recluses the intrigue turns, with interviews, preparations, and a panic. Aimard's South American tales mixed gaucho warfare with convent mystery for European readers.
47515-ulric-the-jarl-a-story-of-the-peni:
Ulric the Jarl is a Viking tale by William Stoddard, printed in London in 1899. Its subtitle calls it a story of the penitent thief. A plate cries, the token of Hilda. The chapters open around the Viking house-fire, with the going out of the ice.

The launching of the ship Sword follows, and her fight with the Ice King. The unknown thing, the living sand, and the Saxon shore carry Ulric west and south. A trireme is taken, the Druids make a great sacrifice, and Lars the Old passes. Hilda of the hundred years, a Jew and a Greek, and a storm in the Middle Sea lead toward Carmel and Esdraelon. In the Northland, Stoddard says, lay the roots of the great nations. His tale runs a Norse sea rover into the world of the Gospels.
4796-jack-tier-or-the-florida-reef:
James Fenimore Cooper, author of The Pilot and Red Rover, wrote Jack Tier, or The Florida Reef. His preface explains that the work already appeared in Graham's Magazine under the title Rose Budd. The change of name was solely the author's act, arising from conviction that the new appellation suits the book better than the one laid aside.

Cooper adds that writing to a name, instead of getting a name from the book's own incidents, caused this departure from ordinary rules. When the book began, most people supposed the Mexican war would end after a few months of hostilities, but Cooper always looked forward to a protracted struggle. Even after Congress began to interfere, he saw as little probability of its ending as on the day it commenced. Readers get a Cooper sea tale set on the Florida reef, first known as Rose Budd.
50417-the-americans-in-the-great-war-v-3:
The Americans in the Great War, volume three, covers the Meuse-Argonne battle: Montfaucon, Romagne, and Sainte Menehould. It belongs to the Michelin Illustrated Guides to the Battlefields, covering 1914 to 1918. Michelin published it in France, London, and the United States after the war.

The Michelin guides were made for visitors to the battlefields, above all for Americans coming to see where their army fought. This volume treats the greatest American battle of the war, in the autumn of 1918. Its named places run from the Montfaucon heights to the Romagne cemeteries and the Argonne forest edge. Maps, routes, and the road numbers that made Michelin famous are the guide working tools. Readers get a battlefield guidebook from the first years of battlefield touring, when the graves were fresh and the villages still ruins.
58673-it-takes-a-thief:
Walter Miller wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Worlds of If in May 1952. It opens with an old Martian legend of gods who rode down in firebirds and kindled air beneath the soil of Mars. Against that myth stands Asir, a young thief tied to a post to die.

Asir hangs by nails through his arms while the knifeman waits, calm, and plays at mumblety-peg with his blade. The youth spits defiance and stares at hills green with trees the old fathers brought. Miller builds a hard, strange Mars where theft, faith, and death meet. The tale asks whether the old gods were as clever as men claim.
59129-the-early-history-of-english-poor-:
The Early History of English Poor Relief, by Leonard, was published at Cambridge in 1900. Leonard had been a student of Girton College. She gives the book to William Cunningham, fellow and lecturer at Trinity College, Cambridge, in thanks for many kindnesses.

In her preface she says the account is chiefly drawn from the city records of London and Norwich. Reports of the justices of the peace among the state papers supply much more. The Privy Council register, orders of council and justices, and a few overseers accounts in the British Museum add the rest. A fairly good system of relieving the destitute by public authority, she notes, has existed in England without break since the seventeenth century. Readers get a scholar history of how England learned to relieve its poor.
65210-never-trust-a-thief:
Never Trust a Thief is a science fiction tale by Ivar Jorgensen, printed in Imagination Stories of Science and Fantasy in February 1958. Its hero, Kiley, is a thief who has just looted a world with the help of an alien guide. Rare gems worth two million stellors fill the back of his ship.

Thaklaru, the alien, speaks straight into Kiley's mind and warns that the first rule in thievery is never to trust an accomplice. Kiley knows the alien may seize the ship, yet he needs its help to get away. The tale is a tight game of greed and doubt played out between a man and a voice in his head.
65608-the-great-green-diamond-or-thief-a: The Great Green Diamond, or thief against thief, is a detective novel in a weekly library of crime tales. The publishers boast of the line in high terms. Every book is a wonder of its kind, they claim, with sound plots that hold readers in breathless hope. Not blood and thunder tales, they insist, but tales of the detection of crime. Nick Carter and Old Spicer are the star names. A green diamond, and thief set against thief, give this number its stakes.
70124-the-war-chief:
Edgar Rice Burroughs wrote The War Chief, a tale of Geronimo's Apaches. The book bears a nineteen hundred twenty seven copyright in his name. Go-yat-thlay, the yawner, is Geronimo's name in his own tongue. Shoz-Dijiji rises through its chapters to lead the Be-don-ko-he band.

Strange twin scenes of dancing savages open the bold romance. Caledonian tribes dance by firelight in Britain's dim far past. Rome's walls and Agricola's march will end that free wild age. Far west, the Athapascan folk trek south through dark old woods. Squaws bear the packs while warriors glide ahead. Ages pass in that slow march toward the Apache homeland. The oath of Geronimo, the scalp dance, and raids fill the mid book. Wichita Billings brings the white world's clash into the tale. Love and the war dance wait in the last fierce chapters.
71238-ritual-and-belief:
Ritual and Belief gathers studies in the history of religion by Edwin Sidney Hartland. The London edition is dated nineteen fourteen. A dated preface from the author's Gloucester home stands at the front. Contents open with an essay called Learning to Think Black. A long study of the relations of religion and magic follows, in four parts.

Its parts treat their common root, theories and definitions, development, and divergence. Essays on the boldness of the Celts and a haunted widow follow. The philosophy of mourning clothes and the voice of the stone of destiny take their turns. A list of books cited closes the volume. The opening essay begins with Tylor's chapters on animism. Claims of tribes without religion rest on poor proof, Hartland argues there.
73491-love-in-chief:
Rose Weekes wrote a novel printed in New York and London in 1904. A motto at the front bids a man master his passions, love in chief, and stay loyal to his friends. Chapter heads are drawn from famed lines, such as write me as one who loves his fellow men. The tale opens among people in a rest home or spa like setting.

Five folk sit self absorbed in their own ills on a cane bench, while a sixth leans on the wall and listens. From such scenes the novel builds its test of love, mercy, and honesty. Chapters move through Arden, a thunder shower, talks with an outsider, and a night piece, toward a close of parting and choice.
79558-the-treble-clef:
Edward Booth wrote The Treble Clef, a novel printed at New York in nineteen twenty-four. Booth had written Bella, The Post Girl, and The Doctor's Lass before it. The tale opens in the town of Daneborough on a night in late Victorian November. The mayor gives a children's fancy dress ball for his eldest girl's fourteenth birthday, in a ballroom kept shut all year.

Some town fathers murmur that the ball lowers the office, and stern voters in the mayor's own ward frown on dancing for the young. Chapter heads follow a sausage boy, a chorister, an alderman, and an organist through the tale. Later parts are named the suitor, the dark angel, the choice, and the sacrifice. Music and town rank run through the plot from the first dance.
autobiography-of-a-pocket-handkerchief:
James Fenimore Cooper narrated this novelette through an embroidered pocket-handkerchief, who tells her own life from a French workgirl's needle to American drawing rooms. The story ran in Graham's Magazine in 1843 under Cooper's name, his first serious magazine fiction. The handkerchief begins with Adrienne, the poor Paris embroiderer who made her, then travels through sale, gift, and theft.

Owners come and go, including the social-climbing Halfacre family and their daughter, while the handkerchief comments on fashion, money, and manners. Cooper uses the device to scold French exploitation of seamstresses and American worship of wealth alike. The result is an odd, pointed satire: a society novel told by its most traveled accessory.
barkham-burroughs-encyclopaedia-of-astou:
Barkham Burroughs published this household encyclopaedia in 1889, billing it as a universal assistant and treasure-house of information. The title page counts the goods: five hundred and twenty-one recipes, two hundred and thirty-six remedies, a hundred and fifty themes for debate, Mother Shipton's prophecy, and twenty thousand things worth knowing. How to be handsome and how to distinguish death stand among the promises.

Lists open the volume, including the highest buildings in the world, from Cologne Cathedral down to St. Mark's, Philadelphia. Remedies follow in dead earnest: corns cured with tobacco extract mixed in white pine pitch, and a cough mixture built on camphor, digitalis, poppy syrup, and sulphate of morphia by the spoonful. The book is a time capsule of Victorian self-help, part cookbook, part doctor, part parlour oracle.
beacon-lights-of-history-volume-3-part-2:
John Lord's Beacon Lights of History continues in this second part of the third volume, devoted to the Renaissance and Reformation in the older lecture ordering. Dante opens the lectures, with Lord ranking true poets among the rarest of men and Homer, Dante, Shakespeare, and Goethe at their head. Dante's banishment, Beatrice, and terrible scorn fill the analysis.

Later lectures move through the revival of learning to Luther and the Reformation, urging peoples who obey God rather than man to defy persecution with serene faith. Lord's Protestant sympathies shape the story openly. As popular history the lectures carried thousands of American lyceum listeners from medieval Florence to Wittenberg in a voice built for the platform.
britannica-1911-bem-josef:
Josef Bem (1795–1850) was a Polish soldier born at Tarnow in Galicia and schooled at the Warsaw military school, where mathematics was his strength. He joined a Polish artillery regiment in French service, fought in the Russian campaign of 1812, and won the Legion of Honour in the defence of Danzig.

Bem’s gunnery won the battle of Igany for Poland in the rising of 1830–1831, and he fought at Ostrolenka and in Warsaw’s last defence. Exile in Paris followed, then a wider field in 1848, when he led armies in the Hungarian war in Transylvania. The entry praises his handling of artillery and the speed of his marches above all his other gifts.
britannica-1911-chief:
Chief comes from the French chef, head, from the Latin caput, and it means the head or upper part of anything. In heraldry the chief is the upper part of the shield, taking one third of the whole. Applied to a person, the word names a head man or one with the highest authority. Chieftain, from medieval Latin and Old French forms, carries that same personal sense.

Use of chief or chieftain for a person is mainly confined to the leader of a clan or tribe, the entry says. A second technical use belongs to feudal law and turns on land holding. The phrase in chief describes a tenant who holds his fief direct from the lord paramount. Word origin, shield design, tribal rule and feudal tenure are the four strands gathered under this one short headword.
britannica-1911-chlopicki-gregorz-jozef:
Gregorz Jozef Chlopicki (1772-1854) was a Polish general, and this 1911 Britannica entry follows his service under many flags. He was born in Podolia and schooled by the Basilians at Szarogrod. In 1787 he ran away from school to enlist as a volunteer in the Polish army. He fought through the campaigns of 1792 to 1794 and stood out at Raclawice as an aide to General Rymkiewicz.

He then joined the Italian legion as a major and won public praise for his courage at the storming of Peschiera. More battles in Italy followed. In 1807 he led the first Vistulan regiment at Eylau and Friedland. In Spain his heroism at Epila and at the storming of Saragossa earned him the legion of honour and a baron's rank. Made a general of brigade in 1809, he marched with Napoleon's great army into Russia in 1812 and was badly wounded at Smolensk.
britannica-1911-great-barrier-reef: Great Barrier Reef is a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a vast coral reef off Australia. The reef runs for about twelve hundred miles along the north east coast. A channel lies inside it, kept calm by the reef wall. That calm lane is a prized route for coasting steamers. The reef itself is cut by a number of deep gaps. Ships can pass through those gaps to reach the open sea.
britannica-1911-jirecek-josef:
Josef Jirecek, a Czech scholar who lived from 1825 to 1888, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Vysoke Myto in Bohemia in October 1825. He joined the Prague office of education in 1850. In 1871 he became minister of that department in the Hohenwart cabinet, at the head of Austrian rule.

His work to win equal rights in schooling for the Slav peoples of the empire brought him the ill will of the German side. He sat in the Bohemian diet from 1878 and in the Austrian parliament from 1879. In 1875 his peers made him president of the royal Bohemian academy of sciences. He died at Prague in November 1888. His books in Czech span a store of Czech letters in three volumes, a word book of Czech writers in two, and editions of old Czech works.
britannica-1911-jirecek-konstantin-josef: Konstantin Josef Jireček (1854– ) was a Czech scholar, son of Josef, who taught history at Prague. He entered the service of Bulgaria in 1879. In 1881 he became minister of education at Sofia. In 1884 he became a professor of world history in Czech at Prague. In 1893 he took the chair of Slavonic antiquities at Vienna. Most of his works deal with the past of the southern Slavs and with their books.
britannica-1911-lambeaux-jef:
Jef Lambeaux (1852–1908), Belgian sculptor, was born at Antwerp and studied at the Antwerp Academy of Fine Arts under Jean Geefs. His first work, "War," was exhibited in 1871, followed by a long series of humorous groups, among them "Children dancing," "Say 'Good Morning,'" "The Lucky Number" and "An Accident" (1875). In Paris he executed "The Beggar" and "The Blind Pauper" for the Belgian salons and produced "The Kiss" (1881), generally regarded as his masterpiece.

After visiting Italy, where the works of Jean Bologne much impressed him, he showed a strong taste for effects of force and motion. His later works include the Antwerp fountain (1886), "Robbing the Eagle's Eyrie" (1890), "Drunkenness" (1893), "The Triumph of Woman". "The Bitten Faun" caused a stir at the Liège exposition of 1905, and "The Human Passions" is a colossal marble bas-relief. He died on the 6th of June 1908.
britannica-1911-lauff-josef:
Lauff, Josef, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of a German poet and playwright. Born at Cologne on the 16th of November 1855, he was a jurist's son. He was schooled at Munster in Westphalia in his youth. He joined the army and served as an artillery officer at Thorn.

He rose to captain at Cologne in the year 1890. In 1898 the emperor called him to Wiesbaden as a major. The call let him give his stage gifts to the royal theatre. His first works were epic poems of the Rhine and peasant wars. Tales and novels came in a steady flow after that time. But his fame rests most on his plays for the stage. A cycle on the great kings of his land is named.
britannica-1911-logan-john-shawnee-chief:
John Logan (about 1725-1780), called Tahgahjuté, was a Cayuga-born leader among the Shawnees. His father, Shikellamy, had been a white child taken and raised by Indians. The name Logan honoured James Logan, Penn's secretary and friend to the tribes. John lived by the Ohio from about 1770 and wed into the Shawnee.

Peace with whites held till April 1774. Greathouse's band then killed kin of Logan, his sister among them. Logan laid the blame on Captain Cresap and sent a war note. Lord Dunmore's War followed. After Point Pleasant he shunned the peace talks. His speech sent to Dunmore won wide fame. Jefferson set it above Demosthenes and Cicero in his Notes on Virginia. Drink took hold in his last years. A nephew killed him near Lake Erie in 1780, after Logan struck at the man.
britannica-1911-micah-thief:
Micah is a Bible article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the man of the hill country of Ephraim whose stolen silver stands behind the shrine at Dan. The tale is told in the book of Judges. Micah stole eleven hundred pieces of silver from his mother, and when she laid a curse on the unknown thief he gave the money back. She then hallowed the silver to Yahweh, and a carved image was made from it.

He first set one of his sons to serve as priest. When a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah came by, he gladly set him up as father and priest in the son's place. When the Danites moved north, they stripped the shrine of its gods and carried off the priest to their new home at Laish.
britannica-1911-szabo-von-szentmiklos-jo:
Szabo von Szentmiklos, Jozsef is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Hungarian geologist. He was born at Kalocsa on the fourteenth of March 1822 and died in 1894. His first work in science was an essay on metals, a field in which he had special training. He then settled at Budapest.

There he studied the rocks of the district and printed the results as a geological map in 1858. In 1859 he joined the Austrian Geological Survey as a volunteer. He cared for the trade side of the work as much as the pure science. He also set up surveys of farm land for the Hungarian Geological Institute. In 1862 he became professor of geology and mineral study at Budapest. His later years went mostly to the close study of rocks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bas-relief:
Bas-relief is sculpture worked upon and attached to a flat surface, usually showing about half an object's depth. Alto-rilievo, or high relief, projects figures partly or wholly in the round, as in the Parthenon's metopes, the Elgin Marbles. Mezzo-rilievo rounds figures to half their natural proportions, with no detached parts. Basso-rilievo, low relief, projects very slightly; its finest specimen is the frieze around the Parthenon's cella.

The lowest kind, rilievo-stiacciato, scarcely rises from its surface, working in fine lines, as in Donatello's Florentine Madonnas. Cavo-rilievo, hollow relief, keeps its outline at surface level while its roundness sinks below, a method chiefly Egyptian. Modern work everywhere neglects the old distinctions, favoring independence of method between the pictorial and the plastic. In America, good relief work exists, though sculpture in the round prevails.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-belief:
Belief receives a full philosophical treatment in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, defining assent given on trust rather than on direct proof. The entry separates belief from knowledge, opinion, and doubt, and asks what moves the mind to accept a claim it cannot see for itself. Authority, rather than the claim's own plain evidence, is the key motive it names.

From there the piece weighs how belief works in ordinary life, in science, and in faith, and how far reason can test what authority hands on. It discusses certainty, motives that make assent reasonable, and the line between blind trust and a trust with grounds. The result is a careful map of an everyday act of mind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jan-van-cleef:
Flemish painter Jan van Cleef, born in Guelderland in 1646 and dead at Ghent on 18 December 1716, studied under Luigi Primo, called Gentile, and Gaspard de Craeyer. On Craeyer's death he was commissioned to finish his master's church works. He was also commissioned to complete cartoons for tapestry ordered by Louis XIV. Churches and convents in Flanders and Brabant are rich in his paintings.

As a draughtsman he was splendid and as a colorist good. He was celebrated for drapery management and charming portrayal of children's heads and women's attractive faces. In a school pre-eminent in portraiture, he held a high place. A vast amount of work, all showing his masters' influence and tending more to Italian than Flemish methods, favored scriptural and religious subjects treated simply and broadly. His masterpiece, Nuns Giving Aid during the Plague, hangs at Ghent's Black Nuns convent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joost-van-cle:
Joost van Cleef, called the Madman, was a Flemish painter and brilliant colorist of the sixteenth century. Born at Antwerp about 1520, one of twenty van Cleefs who painted there, he joined the Antwerp Academy, where his father had been a member. He rivaled the Italians in luminous color, though severity and hardness of outline marred his fine draftsmanship.

Kugler placed him artistically between Holbein and Antonio Moro, and his Portrait of a Man at Munich was long credited to Holbein. His painting took him to France, England, and Germany, and Bruyn of Cologne was his pupil. Believing himself unappreciated, he went to Spain, where, furious that a king preferred Titian's pictures to his, his frenzy grew into permanent insanity. Its most distressing feature was his retouching and ruining of finished pictures, until his family restrained him, and he died about 1556.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-van-cl:
Martin van Cleef was a Flemish painter, born at Antwerp in 1520 and dead in 1570. Son of painter William the younger, he worked lifelong in close touch with his brother Henry, who greatly shaped his art. He studied under Franz Floris, the incomparable Floris, and first loved landscape work.

At Henry's urging, he turned wholly to painting figures. He favoured historical subjects, but also won success in genre painting. After a few large Italian-style compositions after Floris, he painted small pictures only, with great spirit and thorough technique. His work was delicate and refined, harmonious in colour, and excellent in draughtsmanship. He painted figures in landscapes of contemporaries like Gilles and Franz Floris, often collaborating with Henry, who added landscape backgrounds to his figure pieces. On many works he painted a small ape as his mark, earning the name Master of the Ape.
doe-osti-3365759-optimization-of-wall-as:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4509, by Nolan Hayes, Anthony Aldykiewicz Jr., Gavin Mabe, Mikael Salonvaara, and Diana Hun, optimizes wall assemblies for manufactured homes under the DOE Efficient New Homes Program. The study covers HUD Climate Zones 2 and 3, the hot southern belt. Program rules set wall insulation targets such as R-13 and R-21, and factories need buildable ways to hit them.

Options were calculated, down-selected, and then built at pilot scale in a plant. One option swaps oriented strand board sheathing for one inch of insulated sheathing rated R-6; another pairs thinner insulated sheathing with insulated cladding. Window detailing for exterior continuous insulation gets its own chapter, since thickness changes complicate openings. Installers and managers fed back on the pilot builds, grounding the recommendations in factory practice.
essays-on-the-stage-preface-to-the-campa:
Two prefaces from the 1690s stage quarrel come together in Essays on the Stage, an Augustan Reprint Society reprint of March 1948 introduced by Joseph Wood Krutch. Thomas D'Urfey's familiar preface to The Campaigners, his comedy acted at the Theatre-Royal and printed in 1698, answers a late reformer of the stage, Jeremy Collier. The second piece fronts the 1699 translation of Bossuet's Maxims and Reflections upon Plays.

D'Urfey pleads case by case: the ass brought on in his epilogue, he swears, was no mockery of Balaam's miracle, whatever Collier charged at page 199. His preface ends with a satirical fable of the dog and the otter. The pair preserves the Collier controversy from both ends, playwright and churchman.
govdocs-archive_org-noiuf787_gmx_ADL_Ugl:
The Ugly Truth About the ADL is a polemic against the Anti-Defamation League, and it opens with a real scandal. In January 1993, San Francisco police sergeant Tom Gerard and longtime ADL operative Roy Bullock came under FBI scrutiny.

The two were accused of selling illegally obtained information to agents of South Africa, and the case gave the ADL's critics a documented episode to build on. The book builds outward from there into a broad attack on the organization. It is anti-ADL literature, presented as an archive holding without endorsement, for readers studying that fight.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_dnsa-int:
In October 1975 the head of the CIA's MKULTRA program gave top secret testimony about the agency's drug experiments. Michael Evans edited this briefing book, posted in October 2025, fifty years later. MKULTRA explored LSD and other drugs as tools for intelligence work.

The witness conceded that the CIA had as many failures as successes in that research. Testimony of this kind matters because so many MKULTRA files were destroyed. What survives in a sworn record lets readers hear the program described by the man who ran it, in his own careful words, rather than through later rumor.
jack-tier-or-the-florida-reef:
James Fenimore Cooper's Jack Tier; Or, The Florida Reef first appeared in Graham's Magazine as Rose Budd. Cooper explains the change of name in his preface. The Mexican War, still raging as he wrote, colours the whole tale. He defends the war's conduct while praising the Mexican people's mild character.

The brig Molly Swash sails for the Florida reef with a cargo that invites suspicion. Captain Spike, the mysterious Harry Roun, and the sailor Jack Tier drive the plot. Jack, a small red-faced tar with a past, is in truth a woman in disguise, long following the captain who wronged her. Wrecks, smuggled munitions, and the Dry Tortugas supply the action. Cooper's last sea tale mixes war politics with a strange story of devotion and revenge among the reefs.
the-reef:
Edith Wharton opens with a telegram that hammers through George Darrow's train ride from Charing Cross to Dover. Anna's message cites an unexpected obstacle and asks him not to come until the thirtieth, putting him off for the second time with a reasonable excuse.

Darrow and Anna Leath had met again in London three months earlier after twelve years apart, her smile bright against widow's mourning at an embassy dinner. His certainty that her reason will prove good is exactly what chills him. Wharton turns a delayed visit into a study of restraint, pride, and revived love.
the-story-of-louis-riel-the-rebel-chief:
Joseph Edmond Collins published this life of Louis Riel in Toronto in 1885, the year of the North-West resistance. Chapter one writes Riel's life along the Red River. Its banks cross plains bright with wild flowers in summer. Fierce storms sweep them in winter. The country was dyed with blood so often, Collins says, that Red River became its name.

Collins promises to do even this apostle of insurrection the justice that is his right, and begins by disputing the common supposition about Riel's ancestry. Collins draws on Tassé's book on Canadians in the North West. He uses passages in translation. He traces Riel's father and grandfather to Berthier in French Canada. The rebel's Indigenous descent, he argues, was smaller than rumour claimed. The defence uses the racial language of its time.
